Taqwa watch face · the Moon style · your call

Where the Moon keeps your slots

Arch, Ring and Sun keep the wearer's two slots along the bottom. The approved Moon puts one slot at nine instead. A watch face can't move a slot from one style to another, so the Moon has to choose: keep its drawing (a), or bring both slots to the bottom with the others (d).

Cape Town, Sunday 18 October 2026, 6 Jumada al-Ula 1448, as in the approved mockups. The battery (82%) and the step count (6,410) stand in for whatever the wearer picks.

Screen
a

Keep today's drawing

The Moon stays as you approved it: a filled left slot shows in the ring at nine, and the right slot never shows. But the watch keeps both slots' places at the bottom, the same on every style. So the face editor outlines them at the bottom, over the Hijri date, not at nine; and once they are filled, a tap on the ring at nine does nothing, the left half of the Hijri date opens the battery, and the right half opens the steps, which the Moon never draws.

(a) Outlines and taps, once both slots are filled

  1. 1The ring at nine shows the battery, but a tap there opens nothing.
  2. 2The editor outlines this box for the battery, and a tap on the left of the Hijri date opens it.
  3. 3This box is outlined too: a tap on the right of the Hijri date opens the steps, which are drawn nowhere.
d

Redraw the lower half

With both slots empty the Moon is today's drawing, line for line. Fill one and its lower half re-lays, the way Arch, Ring and Sun move their centre up: the moon window rises a little, the Hijri date tucks under it on a tighter curve, and both slots curve along the bottom between the five and seven o'clock indices, inside the same boxes as on the other styles. The editor outlines what you see, a tap opens the value under your finger, and nine o'clock is a plain index.

(d) Outlines and taps, once both slots are filled

  1. 1The battery: outlined where it is drawn , and a tap on it opens it.
  2. 2The steps: the same. Nothing else on the face opens a slot.

(d) in Arabic, 12-hour

A Libyan phone set to 12 hours. The prayer reads right to left and its time follows the phone's clock; the slots keep their places, as on the other styles.

What (d) changes, and what it costs

  • Both slots empty: nothing. The face draws today's Moon.
  • A slot filled: the moon window rises 11 px, and the Hijri date's curve tightens from a 160 to a 132 px radius, so it sits just under the moon and stays out of the slots' boxes.
  • The slots curve along the bottom just inside the hour indices, the six o'clock index between them, each with its source's icon. The value is in ExtraBold at the size of the ring at nine, and a long value steps down to fit, as on the other styles. Always-on, the values dim to mist and the icons to slate.
  • Nine o'clock loses its ring and is a plain index again.
  • One thing stays as today: in the face editor, while both slots are empty, their outlines cross the foot of the Hijri date. They mark where the slots will draw, and the date moves up as soon as one is chosen.
  • To build: a second, compact copy of the moon window and the Hijri date, switched by the slots' type (the face already reads one slot's data from another), and the Moon's own drawing inside slots 4 and 5: a curved text and a turned icon, both already on the Moon. None of it is built yet; it needs a round on the face tools and a Moon pass on the emulator.

My lean: (d). It is the only form in which every outline and every tap is true, and it leaves your approved Moon untouched until a wearer fills a slot.

Drawn with faces.js, the approved mockups' own code: (a) is its Moon, unchanged; (d) is a copy of it with only the lower half redrawn, and this page checks that the copy draws today's Moon exactly when the change is off. faces.js writes the battery as 82%; the watch's own battery source sends 82 with no % sign, and the step counter sends no icon. Both options use faces.js's forms, so only the slot design differs. Add #check to the address to see the measured fit.
